Node 10: its right branch is empty (height −1) and its left branch has height 0, so bf = −1 − 0 = −1.
Node 25: its right branch is empty (height −1) and its left branch is empty (height −1), so bf = −1 − (−1) = 0.
Node 20: its right branch has height 0 and its left branch has height 1, so bf = 0 − 1 = −1.
Node 50: its right branch is empty (height −1) and its left branch is empty (height −1), so bf = −1 − (−1) = 0.
Node 40: its right branch has height 0 and its left branch is empty (height −1), so bf = 0 − (−1) = +1.
Node 30: its right branch has height 1 and its left branch has height 2, so bf = 1 − 2 = −1.
workedExample.outro: Every balance factor is −1, 0 or +1: this is an AVL tree.

workedExample.intro: A model explanation, one step at a time.
steps: A search makes one comparison per level, so it needs at most height + 1 comparisons.
Each comparison rules out one branch and everything in it: decrease and conquer.
The AVL rule keeps the height at most roughly 1.44 log(n + 2) − 1.328.
So with 1,000,000 keys a search needs at most 28 comparisons, compared with up to 1,000,000 in a chain.
Conclusion: search is O(log n) because the AVL rule keeps the path short, not because search uses balance factors.

steps: Is it searched often by key? Yes: names are looked up all day.
Must it stay in order? Yes: it is shown alphabetically.

How often is it updated? Rarely, compared with searches.

workedExample.intro: A model justification: student numbers issued in increasing order and looked up often.
steps: A plain BST would receive the numbers in sorted order and become a chain, with O(n) search.
An AVL tree rebalances after every insertion, so its height stays O(log n).
Every lookup is therefore O(log n): at most 28 comparisons even for 1,000,000 students.
The cost is a stored height in each node and some rotation work on each insertion, which is small next to the number of lookups.
